W01.stem: A shocked dog with isotonic GI losses needs intravascular volume restored. Which fluid type is the most appropriate first choice for resuscitation boluses?

options.B: Half-strength saline with dextrose
options.C: Isotonic crystalloid (e.g. balanced replacement solution or 0.9% NaCl)
options.E: Hypertonic saline as sole long-term maintenance

W01.explanation: Isotonic crystalloids expand ECF/intravascular volume and are first-line for hypovolaemia/shock and most isotonic dehydration. Hypotonic/free-water fluids are for free-water deficit after perfusion is safe — not for resuscitation.

W01.stem: Which statement best matches body-fluid compartments and fluid choice?

options.B: Most total body water is in ICF; isotonic crystalloids mainly expand ECF
options.C: Colloids are first-line for simple dehydration in every GP case
options.D: D5W is preferred for shock boluses because dextrose expands plasma
options.E: Free-water deficit should be corrected before treating shock

W01.explanation: TBW is mainly ICF; ECF (interstitial + plasma) is smaller. Isotonic crystalloids expand ECF. Replace the compartment lost: shock → isotonic crystalloid first; free water later if needed.

W01.stem: First step in working up hyponatraemia at membership level is:

options.A: Immediately give hypertonic saline to all dogs with Na <130 mmol/L
options.B: Assess tonicity / osmolality (or clinical osmoles) before volume status
options.C: Restrict free water in every hypovolaemic patient

W01.explanation: Tonicity first: hypertonic (e.g. severe hyperglycaemia), isotonic/pseudohyponatraemia, or true hypotonic. Only then classify hypotonic cases by volume status.

W01.stem: A diabetic dog has marked hyperglycaemia and low measured Na. The most accurate interpretation is:

options.A: True hypotonic hyponatraemia requiring free-water restriction
options.B: Hypertonic hyponatraemia — water drawn into ECF by effective osmoles; treat the osmoles
options.E: Indication for immediate 3% saline regardless of symptoms

W01.explanation: Severe hyperglycaemia (or mannitol) creates hypertonic hyponatraemia by pulling water into ECF and diluting Na. Treat the osmoles; do not manage as primary hypotonic hyponatraemia.

W01.stem: Hypotonic hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (e.g. ongoing GI Na loss) is best managed initially by:

options.B: Loop diuretics to raise Na
options.C: Restoring volume with isotonic crystalloid and stopping ongoing losses
options.D: Immediate chronic correction faster than 20 mmol/L in 24 h

W01.explanation: Hypovolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia needs volume restoration with isotonic crystalloid and control of losses. Free-water restriction fits euvolaemic/hypervolaemic patterns, not volume-depleted patients.

W01.stem: For chronic or unknown-duration hyponatraemia, a safe approximate ceiling for the rise in Na is:

options.B: About 10–12 mmol/L in 24 h
options.D: Correct to normal Na within 6 hours always
options.E: No limit if the patient is eating

W01.explanation: Chronic/unknown-duration hyponatraemia: keep the rise around ~10–12 mmol/L per 24 h to reduce osmotic demyelination risk. Acute symptomatic seizures need urgent but controlled rise, then slow down.

W01.stem: A hypovolaemic dog with Na 165 mmol/L is shocked. First priority is:

options.A: Immediate free-water replacement with D5W boluses
options.B: Restore perfusion with isotonic crystalloid, then replace free water slowly
options.C: Restrict all fluids until Na is normal
options.D: Give insulin + dextrose to lower Na
options.E: Apply Winter’s formula to guide fluid Na

W01.explanation: Hypernatraemia implies free-water deficit, but shock is treated first with isotonic crystalloid. After perfusion is safe, correct free water slowly with fluid Na below patient Na.

W01.stem: Conceptual free-water deficit uses which relationship?

options.B: FW deficit = TBW × ([Na]patient / [Na]desired − 1)

W01.explanation: FW deficit ≈ TBW × ([Na]patient/[Na]desired − 1). TBW is a fraction of body weight (~0.6 × BW often used in adult dogs; lower fractions often for cats/obese). Recheck Na — formulas are a start, not autopilot.

W01.stem: Target rate for lowering Na in chronic hypernatraemia is approximately:

options.A: 25–30 mmol/L fall in the first 12 h
options.B: ~10–12 mmol/L fall per 24 h
options.D: No monitoring needed if using D5W
options.E: Fall of 1 mmol/L per minute until Na 140

W01.explanation: After volume is restored, replace free water slowly, targeting a similar chronic ceiling (~10–12 mmol/L fall / 24 h) with frequent Na checks.

W01.stem: In a blocked cat with K 8.2 mmol/L and bradycardia, calcium gluconate is given primarily to:

options.A: Lower serum potassium by shifting K into cells
options.B: Provide membrane cardioprotection; it does not lower K⁺
options.C: Replace total-body calcium deficit from obstruction

W01.explanation: Calcium gluconate (when indicated) stabilises cardiac membranes. It does not lower K⁺ — you still need measures that shift or remove K⁺ and fix the cause (e.g. relieve obstruction).

W01.stem: Correct priority order for life-threatening hyperkalaemia is best summarised as:

options.A: Remove K first, then ECG, then calcium
options.B: ECG/arrhythmia risk → cardioprotection (Ca if indicated) → drive K intracellularly → remove K / fix cause
options.C: Insulin + dextrose first in every case before assessing the heart
options.D: Bicarbonate as sole therapy for all hyperkalaemia
options.E: Stop monitoring once calcium is given

W01.explanation: Treat the patient (ECG risk) first; Ca for cardioprotection if indicated; then shift K (e.g. insulin + dextrose — off-label; know species/route/frequency from a trusted source); remove K / treat cause; stop K-containing fluids.

W01.stem: Regarding insulin + dextrose for hyperkalaemia in dogs/cats:

options.A: It is licensed at a single standard veterinary dose you must memorise for the exam without a source
options.B: It is commonly used but off-label — only dose if confident of species, route and frequency from a trusted source; monitor glucose
options.C: It permanently removes potassium from the body
options.D: It replaces the need for calcium in bradycardic hyperkalaemia
options.E: It is contraindicated whenever glucose is normal

W01.explanation: Insulin + dextrose shifts K intracellularly but is off-label in dogs/cats. Do not invent doses; confirm species/route/frequency from a source you trust and monitor glucose. It does not remove K from the body.

W01.stem: Mild hypokalaemia in an eating dog is often managed with:

options.B: Oral potassium supplementation if GI tract is usable
options.C: Calcium gluconate as first-line K replacement

W01.explanation: Mild hypokalaemia with a patient that is eating: oral replacement is appropriate. IV KCl in fluids is for moderate–severe or non-eating patients — never as a neat IV push.

W01.stem: Cervical ventroflexion in a cat with weakness should raise strong suspicion of:

options.B: Hypokalaemia (among other differentials)

W01.explanation: Hypokalaemia classically causes weakness and cervical ventroflexion (especially cats), plus ileus/arrhythmias. Check K and concurrent Mag/Phos in DKA-type settings.

W01.stem: When available, which calcium measurement is preferred for clinical decisions?

options.B: Ionised calcium

W01.explanation: Prefer ionised Ca. Total Ca is influenced by albumin and acid–base, so it can mislead.

W01.stem: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany/seizures) is treated acutely with:

options.B: IV calcium; address cause and correct low Mg if present once stable
options.D: 0.9% NaCl as the only therapy needed

W01.explanation: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia needs IV calcium; oral maintenance once stable. Correct concurrent hypomagnesaemia if low. Causes include eclampsia, hypoparathyroidism, EG, pancreatitis, CKD (variable), citrate from massive transfusion.

W01.stem: A dog blood gas: pH 7.25, PCO₂ 28 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L. Best single interpretation using the dog compensation rule of thumb (~0.7 mmHg PCO₂ per 1 mmol/L HCO₃⁻)?

options.B: Metabolic acidosis with roughly appropriate respiratory compensation
options.D: Must use Winter’s formula to decide

W01.explanation: Low pH + low HCO₃⁻ = metabolic acidosis. Fall in HCO₃⁻ ~12 mmol/L from ~24 → expected PCO₂ fall ~0.7×12 ≈ 8–9 mmHg from ~40 → ~31–32; measured 28 is in a plausible compensated range (exact baselines vary). Do not use Winter’s formula in dogs.

W01.stem: Which statement about acid–base compensation is correct for membership exams?

options.A: Winter’s formula should be applied routinely to dogs
options.B: Cat compensation rules are less established — be cautious applying dog numbers to cats
options.C: Dogs never show respiratory compensation for metabolic disorders
options.D: PCO₂ never changes when HCO₃⁻ changes
options.E: Mixed disorders are excluded if pH is abnormal

W01.explanation: Dog rule of thumb ~0.7 mmHg PCO₂ per 1 mmol/L HCO₃⁻ for metabolic disorders. Cat rules are less established. Winter’s formula is a human equation — not for dogs. Far-off compensation suggests a mixed disorder.

W01.stem: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis is most consistent with which category of causes?

options.A: Diarrhoea alone as the classic normal-AG picture
options.B: Lactate, ketones, uraemic acids, toxins (e.g. ethylene glycol)
options.C: Aggressive chloride-rich fluid as the primary AG-raising mechanism

W01.explanation: High AG ≈ unmeasured anions: lactate, ketones, uraemic acids, toxins (e.g. EG). Normal AG (hyperchloraemic): diarrhoea, RTA, chloride-rich fluids.

W01.stem: Hypoalbuminaemia can mislead anion-gap interpretation because it:

options.A: Raises AG and always proves high-AG acidosis
options.B: Lowers AG and can mask a high-AG process
options.D: Converts all metabolic acidosis to respiratory alkalosis

W01.explanation: Low albumin lowers the AG and can hide a high-AG acidosis. Always read AG with albumin and the clinical picture.

W01.stem: In an azotaemic dog that has not received fluids/diuretics, USG >1.030 most supports:

options.A: Primary renal failure as the only possibility
options.B: Concentrating ability consistent with pre-renal azotaemia (until other diluting factors apply)

W01.explanation: Concentrated urine supports pre-renal azotaemia: dog USG >1.030, cat >1.035 (absent other reasons for dilute urine). Lower USG with azotaemia suggests renal (or post-renal with secondary injury) until proven otherwise — after excluding diluting factors.

W01.stem: Membership USG cut-offs often cited for supporting pre-renal azotaemia are:

options.B: Dog >1.030 and cat >1.035
options.E: USG is irrelevant once creatinine is high

W01.explanation: Dog USG >1.030 and cat USG >1.035 support pre-renal azotaemia when the patient can concentrate and you have not already diluted them. Do not invent tighter ACVIM numeric cut-offs beyond this teaching point.

W01.stem: Which factor can make urine inappropriately dilute and confound the azotaemia–USG assessment?

options.B: Prior fluids, diuretics, glucocorticoids, DM/DI, medullary washout, hypercalcaemia, liver failure, post-obstructive diuresis
options.C: Eating a normal meal 12 hours earlier only

W01.explanation: Many non-renal factors dilute urine. Interpret USG cut-offs only if the patient can concentrate and you have not already diluted them.

W01.stem: Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia (e.g. SIADH-like or psychogenic water intake) is typically managed by:

options.A: Isotonic crystalloid shock boluses as the main Na-raising strategy
options.B: Free-water restriction and finding the cause

W01.explanation: Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia: restrict free water and identify the cause (SIADH-like, psychogenic intake, etc.). Do not “chase Na” the same way as hypovolaemic loss.

W01.stem: Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (heart failure, liver failure, advanced kidney disease) — best principle:

options.A: Liberally give salt-containing fluid to raise Na
options.B: Treat the primary disease; free-water restriction / careful diuresis as indicated — do not chase Na with more salt water

W01.explanation: Hypervolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia: treat the primary disease; restrict free water / diurese carefully as indicated. More isotonic salt water often worsens the problem.

W01.stem: A lab reports albumin 2.0 g/dL (20 g/L) and a “normal” anion gap in a sick dog with suspected lactic acidosis. Best caution?

options.B: Hypoalbuminaemia may have lowered AG and masked a high-AG process
options.C: Convert albumin to mmol/L before interpreting AG
options.E: USG >1.030 proves the AG is valid

W01.explanation: Dual units: 2.0 g/dL = 20 g/L. Low albumin lowers AG and can hide high-AG acidosis (e.g. lactate). Interpret AG with albumin and clinic.

W01.stem: Matching fluid to loss — pure water deficit / hypernatraemia after volume is restored is best addressed with:

options.B: Hypotonic / free-water sources (e.g. D5W once dextrose metabolised; half-strength saline ± dextrose)

W01.explanation: After perfusion is safe, free-water deficit is replaced with hypotonic/free-water fluids, slowly. Isotonic crystalloids do not preferentially correct pure water deficit.

W01.stem: Which exam trap is correctly stated?

options.A: Calcium gluconate lowers serum K⁺ as its primary effect
options.B: Winter’s formula is validated for dogs and should be used in every metabolic acidosis
options.C: Calcium gluconate ≠ K⁺-lowering therapy; Winter’s formula is not for dogs
options.D: Chronic Na disorders should always be corrected in <6 hours
options.E: Insulin + dextrose doses may be invented freely in answers

W01.explanation: Classic traps: Ca gluconate does not lower K⁺; do not apply Winter’s to dogs; correct chronic Na slowly (~10–12 mmol/L/day); do not invent insulin doses (off-label — know species/route/frequency from a trusted source).

W01.stem: A cat has azotaemia and USG 1.020 after overnight fluids at another clinic. Best interpretation?

options.A: USG 1.020 proves irreversible renal failure in every cat
options.B: Prior fluids may have diluted urine — do not over-read the cut-off without context
options.C: Pre-renal azotaemia is confirmed because cat cut-off is >1.015
options.D: Apply dog compensation rule of 0.7 to USG
options.E: Anion gap replaces USG in cats

W01.explanation: Cat pre-renal support is USG >1.035 when concentrating ability is intact and urine has not already been diluted. Prior fluids confound the assessment.

W01.stem: A dog with suspected ethylene glycol toxicity has high AG metabolic acidosis. Albumin is 1.5 g/dL (15 g/L). Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: “Normal” AG would fully exclude toxins because albumin is low
options.B: High AG fits unmeasured anions (e.g. EG metabolites); low albumin can still blunt AG — integrate labs with history
options.D: First give calcium gluconate to lower the AG
options.E: Use Winter’s formula to calculate EG dose

W01.explanation: Toxins such as EG cause high-AG acidosis. Hypoalbuminaemia (1.5 g/dL = 15 g/L) can lower AG and mask severity — always combine AG, albumin, and clinical context. No invented drug doses here.

W02.stem: A 6-year-old Akita has a routine serum K of 6.8 mEq/L (6.8 mmol/L). The ECG is normal, Na is normal, and the sample was separated 6 h after collection. What is the most likely explanation?

options.B: Pseudohyperkalaemia from high-K erythrocytes and delayed separation

W02.explanation: Akitas and some other Japanese and Korean breeds (Shiba Inu, Jindo) can have high-K RBCs, so delayed separation or haemolysis raises K in vitro. A normal ECG and normal Na fit this. Repeat on promptly separated heparinised plasma.

W02.stem: A blood sample from a domestic shorthair cat is moderately haemolysed. What effect on measured K would you expect?

options.B: Little change, because feline RBCs are low-K

W02.explanation: Most canine and feline erythrocytes contain little K, so haemolysis rarely causes clinically important pseudohyperkalaemia, unlike in humans. Haemolysis can still interfere with other assays.

W02.stem: A cat with a urethral obstruction has K 9.0 mEq/L (9.0 mmol/L), bradycardia and absent P waves. What is the most appropriate FIRST drug?

options.A: 10% calcium gluconate slowly IV with ECG monitoring
options.B: Furosemide IV

W02.explanation: With life-threatening ECG changes, cardioprotection comes first. Then shift K into cells (insulin plus dextrose, off-label) and remove the cause (relieve the obstruction, give fluids).

W02.stem: Which statement about calcium gluconate in hyperkalaemia is CORRECT?

options.A: It lowers K by driving it into cells
options.B: Its effect lasts for many hours
options.C: It restores myocardial excitability without lowering K
options.D: It is contraindicated when the ECG is abnormal

W02.explanation: Calcium raises the threshold potential and restores the gap between resting and threshold potential. Serum K is unchanged and the effect is short-lived, so K-lowering steps must follow.

W02.stem: Which statement about insulin and dextrose for hyperkalaemia in dogs and cats is CORRECT?

options.A: Long-acting insulin glargine SC is preferred
options.B: Regular insulin IV with dextrose, then dextrose in fluids and serial glucose checks; this is off-label use
options.C: Dextrose is unnecessary if the patient is normoglycaemic
options.E: It is the fastest way to protect the myocardium

W02.explanation: Insulin activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and moves K into cells. Total-body K does not change. Dextrose prevents hypoglycaemia, which can occur hours later. Calcium, not insulin, provides immediate cardioprotection.

W02.stem: A cat with CKD has cervical ventroflexion, raised CK and K 2.6 mEq/L (2.6 mmol/L). It is eating well. What is the best long-term management?

options.B: Spironolactone

W02.explanation: Oral K gluconate (or citrate) suits stable, eating cats with CKD. HypoK myopathy (ventroflexion, high CK) responds. Chronic hypoK can also worsen feline renal function.

W02.stem: What is the commonly cited maximum IV potassium infusion rate in dogs and cats?

options.B: 0.5 mEq/kg/h (0.5 mmol/kg/h)
options.E: There is no limit if an ECG is attached

W02.explanation: Faster rates risk cardiotoxicity. Remember that KPhos also contributes K.

W02.stem: A dog's hypokalaemia does not correct despite appropriate KCl supplementation. Which value should you check next?

options.B: Sodium

W02.explanation: Hypomagnesaemia increases renal K wasting, so K will not correct until Mg is replaced.

W02.stem: A dog has a platelet count of 1,200 × 10⁹/L. Serum K is 6.1 mEq/L (6.1 mmol/L) and heparinised plasma K is 4.6 mEq/L (4.6 mmol/L). What is the best interpretation?

options.B: Pseudohyperkalaemia from K released by platelets during clotting

W02.explanation: Platelets release K during clotting, so serum K exceeds plasma K. Heparinised plasma reflects the in vivo value.

W02.stem: A dog with PLE has total Ca 7.2 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) and albumin 1.6 g/dL (16 g/L), with no clinical signs. What is the best next step?

options.B: Measure ionised Ca

W02.explanation: Correction formulas predict iCa poorly in dogs and cats. Low total Ca with hypoalbuminaemia often comes with normal iCa. Note that PLE (e.g. Yorkshire terriers) can also cause true ionised hypoCa and hypoMg, which is why measuring is essential.

W02.stem: Which handling error makes ionised Ca falsely LOW?

options.B: Air exposure of the sample, which lets CO₂ escape and pH rise
options.E: Analysis within minutes at the cage side

W02.explanation: CO₂ loss raises pH, which increases Ca binding to albumin and lowers iCa. Excess liquid heparin and EDTA also give falsely low iCa. True acidaemia raises iCa in vivo.

W02.stem: Which electrolyte pattern suggests K-EDTA contamination of a serum sample?

options.B: ↓K, ↑Ca

W02.explanation: K-EDTA adds K and chelates divalent cations (Ca, Mg). ALP can also read falsely low.

W02.stem: A clinically well 10-year-old Keeshond has high iCa, phosphate 2.5 mg/dL (0.81 mmol/L, low-normal), normal renal values, mid-reference PTH and undetectable PTHrP. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Lymphoma

W02.explanation: A "normal" PTH alongside high iCa is inappropriate, which makes this PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia. Low-normal P fits. Keeshonds are over-represented. In renal secondary HPT, iCa is normal or low with high P.

W02.stem: A dog has high iCa, low PTH, raised PTHrP and a firm perianal mass. What is the most likely cause?

options.B: Primary hyperparathyroidism

W02.explanation: This is humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy. PTHrP suppresses PTH. AGASACA and lymphoma are the classic canine causes, so always do a rectal exam.

W02.stem: What is the most commonly reported cause of ionised hypercalcaemia in cats?

options.B: Idiopathic hypercalcaemia

W02.explanation: Feline idiopathic hypercalcaemia is a diagnosis of exclusion: PTH low-normal, PTHrP negative, vitamin D metabolites unremarkable. Neoplasia and CKD are the next main differentials.

W02.stem: A dog chewed a tube of calcipotriol (psoriasis) cream 2 days ago. Which profile is expected?

options.B: ↑Ca, ↓P, high PTH

W02.explanation: The vitamin D analogue increases GI and bone Ca and P absorption, so PTH is suppressed. The high Ca × P product drives soft-tissue mineralisation and AKI. For example, Ca 15.2 mg/dL (3.8 mmol/L) with P 9.3 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L).

W02.stem: What is the most appropriate initial fluid for a dehydrated dog with severe hypercalcaemia?

options.B: 0.9% NaCl

W02.explanation: It is Ca-free, and the Na load promotes calciuresis. LRS contains Ca. Furosemide is added only after volume repletion. Avoid glucocorticoids before the diagnosis, because they can mask lymphoma.

W02.stem: Why should glucocorticoids be avoided in a hypercalcaemic dog before a diagnosis is reached?

options.B: They may mask or partly treat lymphoma and hinder diagnosis

W02.explanation: Steroids lower Ca in lymphoma and other causes. Given first, they can make cytology or histology non-diagnostic and may induce chemotherapy resistance. Sample nodes, marrow and masses first.

W02.stem: A hyperthyroid cat has facial rubbing and muscle tremors 48 h after bilateral thyroidectomy. iCa is 0.8 mmol/L (3.2 mg/dL). What is the mechanism?

options.B: Iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism from parathyroid damage or removal
options.C: Calcitonin excess from the thyroid remnant

W02.explanation: This is the classic complication after bilateral thyroidectomy. Treat with slow IV calcium gluconate (ECG), then oral calcitriol and Ca while monitoring iCa.

W02.stem: A Chihuahua bitch 2 weeks postpartum has tremors, panting and hyperthermia. iCa is 0.65 mmol/L (2.6 mg/dL). During IV calcium gluconate, which monitoring is MOST important?

options.B: Continuous ECG, stopping or slowing for bradycardia or arrhythmias

W02.explanation: Rapid IV Ca can cause bradycardia, arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Give it slowly to effect while watching the ECG. Then manage the pups (supplementary feeding or weaning) and continue oral Ca.

W02.stem: A Yorkshire terrier with PLE has hypocalcaemia that responds poorly to Ca supplementation. Which disturbance most likely explains this?

options.A: Hypomagnesaemia impairing PTH secretion and action
options.B: Hypernatraemia

W02.explanation: Low Mg reduces PTH release and causes end-organ PTH resistance. Correct Mg as well as Ca, and also check vitamin D status in PLE.

W02.stem: A cat with DKA becomes anaemic with haemolysed plasma 24 h after starting insulin. Glucose is now 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L). Which electrolyte disorder is most likely responsible?

options.B: Hypercalcaemia

W02.explanation: Insulin moves P into cells on top of the total-body depletion. Severe hypoP lowers RBC ATP and causes haemolysis, and cats are prone. Supplement potassium phosphate IV and count its K contribution.

W02.stem: Three days after starting tube feeding, a cat with hepatic lipidosis becomes weak. What is the hallmark electrolyte change of refeeding syndrome?

options.B: Hypercalcaemia

W02.explanation: Feeding-induced insulin release drives P, K and Mg into cells. Thiamine deficiency is also part of refeeding. Start feeding gradually and monitor electrolytes closely.

W02.stem: A dog with a pyloric foreign body has Cl 88 mmol/L, K 2.9 mEq/L (2.9 mmol/L) and HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L. What is the best initial fluid plan?

options.B: Sodium bicarbonate-containing fluid
options.E: Ammonium chloride IV as first line

W02.explanation: This is a chloride-responsive hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. The Cl-rich crystalloid plus K corrects the maintenance factors. Relieve the obstruction.

W02.stem: What is the mechanism of paradoxical aciduria in a dog with gastric-outflow vomiting?

options.B: Volume, Cl and K depletion make the kidney reabsorb Na with HCO₃⁻ and secrete H⁺ despite alkalaemia
options.D: Urinary tract infection with urease-negative bacteria

W02.explanation: Aldosterone and hypoK increase distal H⁺ secretion. Low filtered Cl limits HCO₃⁻ excretion, so the urine is acidic while the blood is alkalaemic.

W02.stem: A 13-year-old cat has hypokalaemia, systemic hypertension and metabolic alkalosis that persists despite 0.9% NaCl. Urine Cl is not low. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Gastric outflow obstruction
options.D: Diuretic-induced alkalosis after the drug has been stopped

W02.explanation: Mineralocorticoid excess causes Cl-resistant alkalosis with K wasting. Saline does not fix it. Treat the cause (spironolactone, amlodipine for BP, ± adrenalectomy).

W02.stem: A dog has metabolic alkalosis with HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L. Using illustrative baseline values of HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L and PCO₂ 37 mmHg (4.9 kPa), what is the approximate expected PCO₂ with appropriate compensation?

options.B: 41 mmHg (5.5 kPa)

W02.explanation: ΔHCO₃⁻ = 12 mmol/L, × 0.7 ≈ 8.4 mmHg, so ≈ 37 + 8.4 ≈ 45 mmHg. A measured PCO₂ well above or below this suggests a concurrent respiratory acidosis or alkalosis.

W02.stem: Which statement about assessing respiratory compensation in dogs is CORRECT?

options.A: Winter's formula is validated for dogs
options.B: Canine-derived rules apply: ≈0.7 mmHg PCO₂ change per 1 mmol/L HCO₃⁻ change in metabolic disorders; Winter's formula (human) should not be used
options.C: Dogs do not compensate for metabolic alkalosis
options.E: Feline rules are identical and well validated

W02.explanation: Use species-specific expectations. Compensation never fully normalises pH. Feline data are limited.

W02.stem: A vomiting dog in hypovolaemic shock has HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L (normal), AG 30 mmol/L, Cl 92 mmol/L (low) and lactate 6 mmol/L (54 mg/dL). What is the best interpretation?

options.B: Mixed high-AG metabolic acidosis (lactic) plus metabolic alkalosis (gastric loss)

W02.explanation: A high AG means acid has been added. A normal HCO₃⁻ despite that means a concurrent alkalosis. Low Cl points to gastric HCl loss.

W02.stem: A dog on potassium bromide has a chemistry panel showing Cl 135 mmol/L (high) and a negative anion gap. What is the best explanation?

options.B: Bromide measured as chloride by the analyser, giving falsely high Cl and a low AG

W02.explanation: Many Cl methods cannot tell bromide from chloride. Interpret Cl and the AG with caution in dogs on KBr.

W03.stem: First step in interpreting a full chemistry panel at membership level?

options.A: Rank every analyte by how far it is from the midpoint of the RI
options.B: Compartmentalise by organ/metabolic groups, then synthesise with hemogram and UA
options.C: Order bile acids before reading anything else
options.D: Average all liver enzymes into one “liver score”

W03.explanation: Systematic compartmentalisation (kidney, electrolytes/acid–base, protein, liver leakage vs cholestasis, muscle, glucose/minerals) then integration with hemogram/UA. Not a flat ranked list.

W03.stem: A dog has ↑↑AST, normal ALT, ↑↑CK, normal ALP/GGT/bilirubin. Best interpretation?

options.B: Primary hepatocellular necrosis only

W03.explanation: AST is shared by liver and muscle; CK confirms muscle. Normal ALT/cholestasis markers argue against primary hepatobiliary disease as the driver.

W03.stem: Which finding best supports a regenerative anaemia in a dog?

options.B: Increased absolute reticulocyte count with polychromasia on smear
options.C: A single nucleated RBC on the smear

W03.explanation: Absolute reticulocytes + polychromasia indicate marrow response. nRBC alone and indices alone are insufficient.

W03.stem: In cats, which reticulocyte population should be used to classify regeneration?

options.B: Aggregate reticulocytes

W03.explanation: Aggregate reticulocytes (and polychromasia) reflect current regeneration; punctate persist longer and mislead if used alone.

W03.stem: Anaemia detected 24 hours after acute haemoperitoneum, low absolute reticulocytes. Best statement?

options.B: May be pre-regenerative; marrow often needs ~3–5 days

W03.explanation: Early haemorrhage/haemolysis can appear non-regenerative until the marrow responds (~3–5 days).

W03.stem: Regenerative anaemia plus spherocytes and agglutination in a dog most strongly suggests?

options.B: Anaemia of inflammatory disease

W03.explanation: Spherocytes ± agglutination with regeneration classic for canine IMHA (confirm smear, saline agglutination technique, rule-outs).

W03.stem: Schistocytes in a regenerative or non-regenerative anaemia suggest which mechanism?

options.B: Fragmentation / microangiopathic injury

W03.explanation: Schistocytes indicate RBC fragmentation (microangiopathy, turbulence, some neoplasias/DIC contexts).

W03.stem: Most consistent leukocyte change in a classic stress leukogram?

options.B: Lymphopenia
options.C: Marked left shift with toxic change

W03.explanation: Lymphopenia is the most consistent stress (corticosteroid) marker; mature neutrophilia and eosinopenia often accompany it.

W03.stem: Which set best fits an inflammatory leukogram?

options.A: Mature neutrophilia, lymphopenia, no bands, no toxic change only
options.B: Neutrophilia or neutropenia with left shift ± toxic change

W03.explanation: Inflammation: left shift ± toxic change; neutrophil count may be high or low depending on demand vs supply.

W03.stem: A dog has neutropenia with bands ≥ segmented neutrophils and toxic change. This is most concerning for?

options.B: Demand exceeding supply (serious inflammatory demand)

W03.explanation: Degenerative left-shift pattern (bands ≥ segs and/or neutropenia with immaturity) suggests tissue demand outpacing marrow release—clinically serious.

W03.stem: Physiologic (epinephrine) leukocytosis is best characterised by?

options.A: Long-standing neutrophilia with toxic left shift
options.B: Short-lived neutrophilia ± lymphocytosis without left shift
options.E: Identical to stress leukogram including lymphopenia

W03.explanation: Brief catecholamine shift; common in cats/excited patients; no left shift/toxic change; may show lymphocytosis (unlike stress).

W03.stem: Hyperproteinaemia with albumin 4.8 g/dL (48 g/L) and proportional globulin rise most often means?

options.B: Dehydration / haemoconcentration

W03.explanation: ↑Albumin is not produced in excess in myeloma—think water deficit/haemoconcentration first.

W03.stem: Albumin 1.6 g/dL (16 g/L) with low globulins, diarrhoea, and non-azotaemic patient most suggests?

options.B: Protein-losing enteropathy (or combined enteric loss)

W03.explanation: Panhypoproteinaemia with GI signs fits PLE/severe enteric loss (also consider haemorrhage/exudate). PLN more often albumin-selective early.

W03.stem: Best next step when dipstick protein is positive in a dog you suspect has renal proteinuria?

options.B: Confirm and quantify with UPC (preferably quiet sediment)

W03.explanation: Dipstick is a screen (albumin-biased); UPC quantifies. Interpret with sediment, USG, and clinical context; exclude post-renal causes.

W03.stem: Low A:G ratio alone proves which diagnosis?

options.B: Nothing by itself — interpret absolute albumin and globulin with the patient

W03.explanation: A:G is a clue only; many processes lower the ratio (↓alb and/or ↑glob).

W03.stem: Which pattern best supports cholestasis rather than pure hepatocellular leakage?

options.B: ↑ALP and ↑GGT ± hyperbilirubinaemia

W03.explanation: ALP/GGT (± bilirubin) mark cholestasis/induction pathways more than ALT alone.

W03.stem: Regarding ALP in cats versus dogs, which is correct?

options.A: Cats show marked steroid-induced ALP like dogs
options.B: Feline ALP has a short half-life; elevations warrant investigation
options.C: ALP is never useful in cats
options.D: Any ALP rise in dogs proves bile duct obstruction
options.E: GGT is always higher than ALP in feline lipidosis

W03.explanation: Cats: short ALP half-life → take rises seriously; they lack typical canine steroid ALP induction. Lipidosis often ALP↑ with relatively modest GGT—pattern, not absolute rule.

W03.stem: Dog on corticosteroids: ALP ↑↑, GGT normal/mild, ALT mild, bilirubin normal, clinically well. Most reasonable statement?

options.A: Emergency biliary surgery indicated by ALP alone
options.B: Consider steroid induction of ALP among differentials; interpret clinically
options.E: Rules out any hepatobiliary disease forever

W03.explanation: Canine ALP is sensitive and inducible by steroids; integrate GGT, bilirubin, clinical status—do not operate on ALP alone.

W03.stem: Bilirubinuria in a cat is best regarded as?

options.A: Often normal in male cats like dogs
options.B: Abnormal and worthy of explanation (haemolysis or hepatobiliary disease)
options.D: An artefact of concentrated urine only
options.E: Equivalent to a positive leukocyte esterase

W03.explanation: Any bilirubinuria in cats is abnormal; dogs (especially males) may show low-grade bilirubinuria less alarmingly.

W03.stem: Which UA statement is safest at membership level?

options.B: Leukocyte esterase/nitrite reliably diagnose canine/feline UTI
options.C: Confirm unexpected glucosuria and interpret proteinuria beyond the strip (sediment ± UPC)
options.D: Ketone pads detect all β-hydroxybutyrate perfectly

W03.explanation: Dipstick has species and analyte pitfalls; refractometer for USG; sediment ± culture for UTI; UPC for significant proteinuria.

W03.stem: Haematuria vs haemoglobinuria vs myoglobinuria — dipstick “blood” positive. What helps differentiate?

options.B: Sediment (RBCs), plasma colour, and clinical CK/muscle context

W03.explanation: Pad detects haeme; sediment RBCs support haematuria; clear plasma + pigmenturia with muscle injury/↑CK supports myoglobin; haemolysed plasma supports haemoglobinuria.

W03.stem: Concordant ↑HCT, ↑TP, and albumin 4.5 g/dL (45 g/L) in a vomiting dog most likely reflects?

options.B: Haemoconcentration from dehydration

W03.explanation: Parallel rises in red cell mass estimate and proteins support dehydration/haemoconcentration—confirm on exam.

W03.stem: Anaemia of inflammatory disease is typically?

options.B: Mild to moderate and non-regenerative (or poorly regenerative)

W03.explanation: Common, usually mild–moderate, non-/poorly regenerative; mechanisms involve iron sequestration and cytokine marrow suppression.

W03.stem: Absolute neutrophil count matters more than the neutrophil percentage because?

options.A: Percentages ignore total WBC and mislead when leukopenia/leukocytosis present
options.B: Analysers never report absolutes
options.D: Stress leukograms only appear on percentages

W03.explanation: Always interpret absolute differential counts.

W03.stem: Marked hyperglobulinaemia, rouleaux, and clinical hyperviscosity suspicion — next conceptual step?

options.B: Consider monoclonal gammopathy work-up (protein electrophoresis pathway) after excluding common polyclonal causes as appropriate

W03.explanation: Marked globulin increases raise polyclonal vs monoclonal differentials; SPE (and further typing) when clinically indicated.

W03.stem: Glucose pad positive on urine, serum glucose 90 mg/dL (5 mmol/L). Best consideration?

options.B: Consider primary renal glucosuria / tubular dysfunction (e.g. Fanconi) or strip artefact—verify

W03.explanation: Glucosuria without hyperglycaemia suggests renal tubular leak or false-positive strip—confirm methods/history.

W03.stem: Which pair is the better “liver function” reflection than ALT?

options.A: Albumin and coagulation factors (with clinical context)
options.B: ALP isoform percentage alone

W03.explanation: Enzymes = injury/induction; function ≈ synthetic/excretory markers (albumin, glucose, urea, cholesterol, bilirubin, coag ± bile acids/ammonia).

W03.stem: Active urine sediment (pyuria, haematuria) while measuring UPC — best practice comment?

options.A: UPC is unaffected—always trust for staging glomerular disease
options.B: Lower urinary inflammation/haemorrhage can confound UPC; note and often recheck after addressing
options.C: Dipstick protein is preferable to UPC here

W03.explanation: Post-renal protein/blood inflates UPC; interpret cautiously with active sediment.

W03.stem: Dog: non-regenerative anaemia, azotaemia with creatinine 3.0 mg/dL (≈265 µmol/L), inadequately concentrated urine, normal leukogram. Most coherent clin-path story?

options.B: Anaemia consistent with chronic kidney disease (among differentials)

W03.explanation: CKD commonly causes non-regenerative anaemia (↓EPO ± inflammation/iron issues) with azotaemia and inappropriate USG. Still a differential list, not a sole proof.

W03.stem: Which approach best integrates fluid status with clin path without re-teaching Na/K physiology?

options.A: Diagnose dehydration from sodium alone always
options.B: Use concordant HCT + TP/albumin + physical exam; electrolytes as corroboration
options.C: Ignore albumin if HCT is normal
options.E: Use leukocyte esterase as hydration marker

W03.explanation: Haemoconcentration pattern (↑HCT + ↑TP/albumin) plus exam findings; Na/K patterns from prior weeks corroborate free-water/solute status but are not used in isolation.
